article.title: Dinner Party Wine Etiquette: What to Bring and What to Expect
article.body:
Dinner Party Wine Etiquette: What to Bring and What to Expect

No, bringing wine to a dinner party is not rude. In the UK it is polite and expected, but treat the bottle as a gift for the host rather than a contribution to the meal, so the host does not have to open it that evening. Drinks House 247 suggests bringing something you would happily drink yourself.

Most of the awkwardness around wine at dinner parties comes from one misunderstanding: is the bottle you bring meant for tonight, or for the host? Once that is clear, everything else falls into place, for guests and hosts alike.

Is the bottle a gift or a contribution?

At a dinner party, where the host has planned and cooked a meal, the bottle you bring is a gift. The host will usually have chosen wines to go with the food, and there is no obligation to open yours that evening. A gift is theirs to enjoy whenever they like.

It is different when the invitation says "bring a bottle". That is a request to contribute to the drinks, and the host will expect to open what guests bring. Informal gatherings, barbecues and parties often work this way.

Reading the invitation

What the host says What it usually means What to bring
"Come for dinner"The host is providing food and drinkA bottle as a gift, for them to keep
"Bring a bottle"Guests are contributing to the drinksA bottle to share, ideally ready to drink that evening
"We're doing fish" or "It's a curry night"A hint about the foodA wine that suits the dish, which the host may choose to open
"Don't bring anything"Politeness, usuallyA small gift anyway: a bottle, flowers or chocolates
"We don't drink"Take it literallyA good non-alcoholic drink, chocolates or flowers

What kind of wine should you bring?

Choose something you would be happy to drink yourself. That is the most reliable test of a good bottle, and it gives you something to say about it. A few styles are almost always welcome:

  • A versatile red: a Rioja Crianza, a Côtes du Rhône or a New Zealand Pinot Noir works with most meals and suits most tastes.
  • A crisp white: a Chablis, an Albariño or a Sancerre goes with fish, chicken and vegetarian dishes.
  • Something sparkling: a bottle of champagne or English sparkling wine feels like an occasion, and it keeps well if the host saves it.
  • A dessert wine or port: a thoughtful choice, especially if you know the host enjoys a cheese course.

If you know your host well, bring something connected to them: a wine from a region they have visited, or a grape they have mentioned they like.

How much should you spend?

There is no rule, and the right amount depends on the occasion and how well you know the hosts. What matters is that the bottle looks considered rather than grabbed on the way. Bringing something far more expensive than the host is likely to serve can make an evening awkward, and bringing the cheapest bottle on the shelf can look careless. Aim for something you would choose for a good dinner of your own.

Should the bottle be chilled?

For a gift, no. A room-temperature bottle signals clearly that it is for later, and it avoids the host feeling they must open it before it warms up. If the host has asked you to bring the fizz for the evening, then bring it cold, and say so when you arrive so it goes straight into the fridge.

What should you say when you hand it over?

Something short that takes the pressure off: "This is for you to enjoy another time." It tells the host they do not need to open it, and it stops anyone wondering. If you think it would suit the meal, you can say that too, and leave the decision to them.

What to avoid

  • Asking for your bottle to be opened. Once handed over, it belongs to the host.
  • Bringing a wine that needs explaining. A very unusual natural wine or an intensely sweet style can be a brilliant gift for the right person and a puzzling one for the wrong one.
  • Arriving empty-handed after being told not to bring anything. A small gesture is still appreciated.
  • Bringing alcohol to a host who does not drink. Choose a good non-alcoholic alternative instead.

If you are the host

Thank the guest, put the bottle somewhere sensible, and do not feel obliged to open it. If it suits the food and you want to share it, open it and say who brought it; guests usually enjoy seeing their choice poured. If you plan to keep it, a simple "I'm going to save this for a special occasion" is gracious and honest. Either way, a short message the next day to say you enjoyed it, or are looking forward to it, is always welcome.

Frequently asked questions

Is it rude to bring wine to a dinner party?

No. In the UK it is polite and expected. Treat the bottle as a gift for the host rather than a contribution to the meal, so there is no obligation for them to open it that evening.

Should the host open the wine a guest brings?

Not necessarily. At a dinner party the host has usually chosen wines for the meal, and a guest's bottle is a gift to keep. If the invitation said bring a bottle, the host will expect to open it.

What wine should you bring to a dinner party?

Something you would happily drink yourself. A versatile red such as Rioja Crianza, a crisp white such as Chablis, or a bottle of champagne suits most hosts and most meals.

Should you chill the wine you bring as a gift?

No. A room-temperature bottle signals that it is a gift for later. Bring it chilled only if the host has asked you to bring wine for the evening.

article.summary: Bringing wine to a dinner party is polite, but it is a gift for the host, who need not open it. What to bring, what to avoid, and how hosts should handle it.
